client: I've been really struggling lately since my partner moved abroad for work about six months ago. It's like this hollow feeling that just sits in my chest most of the time, and even when we video call, it doesn't really feel the same as having them here. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the situation is what it is — they're still going to be thousands of miles away no matter what I say in this room.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds genuinely heavy — that hollow feeling in your chest, the sense that even connection across a screen can't quite fill the space your partner left. I notice something in how you're speaking too, a kind of quiet urgency, like you're holding a lot while also bracing yourself against hope, as if protecting yourself from disappointment by reminding yourself nothing here can change the distance. That thought — *"talking won't change anything"* — makes a lot of sense as a way to guard your heart, but I wonder if we could gently explore whether there might be things that *can* shift, even if the miles stay the same, like how you're relating to this pain and moving through your days with it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that something can shift, but honestly it just feels like words right now. Like, the apartment is still going to be quiet when I get off this call, and he's still going to be six time zones away. I guess I'm just not sure what "relating to the pain differently" even looks like in practice, because every time I try to distract myself or think positively, it just feels fake.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of tension in your voice — tells me this isn't resignation, there's actually a lot of feeling pressing up against those words, even as they sound measured and careful. And you're naming something really important: forced positivity *does* feel fake, because it is — it skips over the grief rather than actually meeting it. What I'd want to explore with you isn't "thinking positively" but something quieter, like learning to sit in that silent apartment without the silence meaning *abandoned* — because right now it sounds like the quiet is confirming a story, and that story might be worth looking at together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I mean... you're right that the silence does something to me. It's not just quiet, it's like the apartment is actively reminding me that no one chose to be there, no one is coming home, and that feels like evidence of something. I guess I'm just not sure how you "look at" a story like that without it just... confirming itself all over again.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, quickly, with a kind of tightness — sounds like someone trying to hold something fragile together while also bracing for it to break, and that makes sense given what you just named. You've identified something really central to CBT: that thought — *"no one chose to be there"* — isn't just a feeling, it's a conclusion, and it's worth asking gently whether it's the only interpretation the evidence supports, or whether it's the one grief is most loudly offering right now. Because your partner choosing to stay connected across six time zones, the calls, the relationship still existing — that's also evidence, and the story the silence tells isn't necessarily the truer one.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know logically you're right that my partner staying in touch is evidence of something real. But in those moments when the silence stretches out and I'm sitting alone in this apartment at 11pm, logic just doesn't reach me the way the loneliness does. It's like the loneliness is louder than any evidence I can think of, and I don't know how to turn down the volume on it.
therapist: There's something really honest and important in what you just said — and the way you said it, softly, almost carefully, like you're describing something tender — tells me this isn't despair so much as a kind of exhausted clarity, you *know* the logic, and you're tired of it not being enough. What you're describing is actually one of the most human parts of grief: that at 11pm, alone, the emotional brain is simply louder than the thinking brain, and that's not a failure of yours to "think correctly." So rather than trying to out-argue the loneliness in those moments, I wonder if we could work on something more like — what might it look like to *acknowledge* it without letting it write the whole story, almost like saying *"yes, I'm lonely right now, and that's real"* without it becoming *"and that means I'm alone forever"*?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually gets it, like intellectually that distinction makes sense. But in the moment, at 11pm when it's quiet and my phone isn't buzzing and I'm just... there... it feels impossible to stop at "I'm lonely right now" without it sliding into something bigger and darker. It's like trying to hold water in your hands, you know the difference between the two thoughts, but you can't actually keep them separate.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly, at a measured pace, but with something almost fragile in your voice — feels like someone who is genuinely trying, holding themselves together carefully while describing exactly how hard that holding is, and I want to honour that effort. Your image of water slipping through your hands is actually perfect, and it tells me something important: we shouldn't be trying to *grip* the thoughts harder, because that's exactly what makes them slide. What if, instead of trying to hold the boundary between "lonely right now" and "alone forever," we worked on building something small and concrete for those 11pm moments — not to stop the slide, but to give you somewhere to land when it happens?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of having somewhere to land, but I'm not sure what that would even look like at 11pm when I'm already in that spiral. Like, what could I actually do that wouldn't just feel like a distraction, something hollow that doesn't really touch the feeling? I guess I'm worried that anything I try will just feel like I'm going through the motions, and that might actually make it worse, make me feel more alone because even my coping strategies feel empty.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now — almost urgent, searching — tells me this question really matters to you, that you're not just being skeptical but genuinely reaching for something real, and that reaching *is* worth noticing. What you're describing isn't a problem with coping strategies, it's actually a really important insight: anything that *bypasses* the feeling will feel hollow, so what we're looking for isn't distraction but something that *meets* you in it. I'm wondering if "somewhere to land" might look less like an activity and more like a small ritual that says *"I see you, this is hard right now"* — something that acknowledges the loneliness rather than tries to paper over it, like writing one honest sentence about how you feel, or even just texting your partner something real in that moment, not to fix it, but to let the feeling point toward connection instead of absence.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually... lands differently than I expected, the part about acknowledging it instead of trying to get rid of it. But I'm not sure about the texting my partner thing — sometimes when I reach out in those moments, I feel like I'm burdening them, and then the guilt just piles on top of the loneliness and it gets worse. The honest sentence idea is interesting, but I'm skeptical I'd actually do it in the moment when everything feels heavy.
therapist: The softness in your voice, even as you're pushing back a little, tells me something shifted just now — there's a small opening there, even alongside the doubt, and that matters. I want to gently hold up that thought about burdening your partner, because that belief — *"my needs are too much, reaching out will hurt them"* — is worth examining, because it may be quietly adding a layer of isolation on top of the loneliness, teaching you to turn away from connection right when you need it most. And on the honest sentence idea — I hear your skepticism, and I'm not asking you to trust it yet, just to notice that the part of you that called it "interesting" is still there, even at the end of a heavy day.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying about the belief that my needs are too much... and honestly, part of me knows it's probably not entirely fair to my partner. But it's hard to just let go of it, because there have been times when I could see them getting drained, and I don't want to be the reason someone I love feels exhausted.
therapist: The softness in your voice, almost careful and a little fragile, tells me this isn't just a belief you've picked up from nowhere — it's something you've built from real moments, real observations, and that makes it feel like *fact* rather than *interpretation*. But I want to gently name what I'm hearing: you love your partner so deeply that you're willing to be alone at 11pm, carrying this by yourself, rather than risk adding to their weight — and while that's a profound act of care, it may also be quietly teaching the loneliness that it has to stay hidden. The question worth sitting with isn't *"are my needs too much?"* but rather *"am I making a decision for my partner that they haven't actually asked me to make?"*
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That question hits somewhere I wasn't expecting it to. Like, I've been so sure I was protecting them, but when you put it that way, it sounds more like I've been making a decision on their behalf without even asking. I guess I'm scared that if I do ask, if I actually let them see how much I'm struggling at 11pm, they'll confirm what I already fear — that it really is too much.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, your voice pitched high and tight — sounds like someone who just touched something they've been carefully avoiding, and there's both fear and a kind of relief in that, like finally saying the real thing out loud. What you just named is the core of it: you're not just afraid of burdening your partner, you're afraid of *confirmation*, that asking will prove the fear true — and so the silence feels safer than the risk. But I want to sit with you in this for a moment, because that fear of confirmation is actually keeping you from the one thing that could genuinely loosen its grip — and your partner hasn't confirmed it yet, which means right now it's still just a fear, not a fact.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right that it's still just a fear and not a confirmed fact. But the thing is, even just thinking about actually asking my partner if they're getting tired of me makes my chest go tight, like I'm about to do something that can't be undone. What if saying it out loud makes it more real, or worse, what if I ask and they hesitate before answering, and that hesitation tells me everything?
therapist: The tightness in your chest, the speed in your voice, the pitch climbing as you described that moment — your whole body is bracing against something it's decided is dangerous, and that physical response is real and worth honouring. But I want to gently name what's happening in that fear of the hesitation: you're already interpreting a pause that hasn't happened yet, already writing your partner's answer before they've spoken — and that's not intuition, that's anxiety filling in the blanks with your worst fear. The question isn't really *"what if they hesitate?"* but *"can I trust myself to stay curious about what a hesitation might mean, rather than letting it confirm a story I've already decided is true?"*
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
